Yews
Conifers whose seeds are partly enclosed by a fleshy aril.
Yew family.
Columelliaceae
A small family of Andean shrubs; tubular flowers occur in several members.
Botanical family Columelliaceae.
Sedges
The sedge family, generally with solid stems and spikelets; the fruit is often an achene enclosed by a perigynium.
Sedge family.
Pitcher-plant family
Carnivorous plants of nutrient-poor habitats, whose leaves can form pitcher traps.
American pitcher-plant family.
Hylocomiaceae
A family of pleurocarpous mosses, often pinnately branched and mat-forming in woodland.
Botanical family Hylocomiaceae.
Orthotrichaceae
A family of acrocarpous mosses often growing on bark and rock, with capsules borne on setae.
Botanical family Orthotrichaceae.
Evening-primrose family
A family including evening-primroses and willowherbs, often with four-parted flowers and capsular fruits.
Evening-primrose family.
Four-o’clock family
A mostly tropical family with often tubular perianths; the persistent perianth base may enclose the fruit.
Four-o’clock family.
Honeysuckle family
A family including honeysuckles, scabious and knautias; flowers are often arranged in heads or cymes.
Honeysuckle family.
New Caledonian austrotaxus
Austrotaxus spicata
Austrotaxus.

A conifer endemic to the humid forests of New Caledonia. Its stiff, leathery linear leaves appear in two ranks; unlike pines, it bears no woody cones. Each seed is partly enclosed by a fleshy red aril.
Humid montane forests of New Caledonia; Kew reports Near Threatened status based on IUCN data.
Small tree with a narrow crown and tiered branches, covered in evergreen leaves.
Flat, leathery linear leaf with a pointed tip and pale stomatal bands beneath.
Small male pollen strobilus; the sexes occur on separate plants.
Single seed partly enclosed by a red aril, not a woody cone.
Curved sedge
Carex curvula
Alpine sedge.

An alpine sedge forming dense tufts of narrow arching leaves. Several dark, closely spaced spikelets rise above the foliage. As in other Carex, the achene is enclosed in a perigynium, a useful character separating sedges from grasses.
Alpine grasslands and turf in European mountain ranges.
Low compact tuft of strap-like leaves and upright flowering culms.
Narrow V-folded leaf with a sheath around the culm.
Closely packed dark brown spikelets with reduced flowers.
Three-sided achene enclosed in a perigynium; shown as separate structures.
Spiny desfontainia
Desfontainia spinosa
Spiny desfontainia.
An evergreen Andean shrub with leathery, holly-like leaves edged in sharp teeth. Its pendent scarlet tubular flowers end in yellow lobes, a distinctive color contrast.
Native to the Andes of South America; RHS notes cultivation in moist, humus-rich soil.
Upright, branching evergreen shrub with dense foliage.
Glossy elliptic leathery leaf with sharp marginal teeth.
Long pendent scarlet tube ending in yellow lobes.
Shown as a green berry; consulted references chiefly document the flower, so this fruit detail is indicative.
Archer’s diselma
Diselma archeri
Cheshunt pine.
A compact conifer of Tasmania’s wet highlands, usually a shrub. Its densely branched rigid sprays bear minute appressed scale leaves in opposite pairs; the tiny female cone has two pairs of scales.
Endemic to wet subalpine heath and forest in Tasmania, mainly around 1,000–1,750 m elevation.
Dense shrub, occasionally a small tree, with fine rigid branching.
Twig covered in tiny obtuse opposite scale leaves.
Small terminal pollen cone; the species is dioecious.
Terminal female cone with persistent scales; the seeds are slightly winged.
Sweet spurge
Euphorbia dulcis
Sweet spurge.

A European perennial spurge with mostly simple upright stems and alternate lanceolate leaves, often blue-green beneath. Its flowers are cyathia, the distinctive inflorescences of spurges, with small nectar glands; the fruit is a three-lobed capsule.
Across much of Europe, in woods, edges and relatively moist grassy places.
Several upright, little-branched stems ending in cyathia-bearing umbels.
Oblong-lanceolate leaf, entire or finely toothed, blue-green beneath.
Cyathium with orange-red nectar glands and no true petals.
Slightly warty three-lobed capsule.
Venezuelan marsh pitcher
Heliamphora nutans
Nodding Heliamphora.

A perennial carnivorous plant of the tepuis of the Guiana Shield. A rhizome produces clumps of upright pitcher leaves; a small nectar-bearing appendage does not close the mouth, and a side slit drains excess water. White flowers nod from a separate stalk.
Mountains of southeastern Venezuela and neighboring Guyana and northern Brazil; wet marshes and rock sheets at high elevations.
Clump of upright tubular traps, green often shaded red, with a separate flowering stalk.
Open pitcher leaf with a small nectar spoon and downward-pointing internal hairs.
White nodding flower with narrow parts on a stalk separate from the pitchers.
Winged seeds with wavy ridges.
Glittering wood-moss
Hylocomium splendens
Staircase moss.

A woodland moss forming loose yellow-olive mats. Its red-brown stems and pinnate branches grow in successive annual tiers, giving it a distinctive feathered, staircase-like appearance. It has no flowers or seeds; it produces spores in capsules.
Widespread in cool boreal and temperate forests of the Northern Hemisphere; common in the understory.
Loose mat of pinnate fronds in successive tiers.
Small pinnate frond bearing many minute leaves.
Mosses do not flower; reproductive structures are slender setae bearing capsules.
Spore capsule; reproduction is by spores, not fruits.
Bitter candytuft
Iberis amara
Annual candytuft, rocket candytuft.

A small branched annual in the mustard family. Lower leaves are spoon-shaped, upper leaves narrower, and broad corymbs carry small white to pale lilac flowers with enlarged outer petals. The flattened, nearly round notched fruit is a silicle.
Native to western and southern Europe; found in dry open ground and disturbed soils.
Branched upright annual with broad terminal corymbs.
Lower spatulate leaf, entire or slightly toothed near the tip.
Four unequal petals, the two outer ones enlarged, characteristic of Iberis.
Flattened round silicle with a narrow wing and apical notch.
Moonflower
Ipomoea alba
White morning-glory.

A vigorous tropical twining vine with large heart-shaped leaves. Its fragrant white funnel-shaped flowers open in the evening and remain open through the night; the outer sepals have long awn-like tips, useful on fruiting material.
Native to tropical and subtropical America; naturalized in other warm regions.
Twining climber on a support, with large alternate leaves.
Broad, entire, heart-shaped blade with an acuminate tip.
Large white funnel-shaped corolla with a long tube and spreading limb, opening at night.
Dry capsule usually containing four dark seeds.
Field scabious
Knautia arvensis
Field scabious.

A perennial with upright stems, often rough and hairy. Basal leaves form a rosette; upper leaves are opposite and often deeply divided. Lilac-blue flower heads consist of many small florets, and each dry fruit retains a bristly calyx.
Widespread across Eurasia in dry to moderately fresh grasslands, pastures, banks and roadsides.
Branched stems of variable height bearing rounded lilac flower heads.
Opposite pinnatifid stem leaf; basal rosette leaves are simpler.
Head of many tubular florets, with peripheral florets often larger.
One-seeded dry fruit with a persistent bristly calyx.
White leadtree
Leucaena leucocephala
Leucaena, white leadtree.

A tropical tree with bipinnate foliage and spherical cream flower heads. Its long flat pods split into two valves and contain several seeds. The plant contains mimosine, which can poison livestock when substantial amounts of forage are consumed; suitable processing is needed for food use.
Native to Mexico and Central America; widely planted and naturalized through the tropics.
Tree with a short trunk, spreading crown and finely bipinnate foliage.
Large compound leaf with many small opposite leaflets on several pinnae.
Globose head of numerous cream flowers with long stamens.
Flat brown pod containing a row of seeds.
Perennial pepperweed
Lepidium latifolium
Broad-leaved pepperweed.

A tall rhizomatous perennial mustard with broad basal leaves and narrower stem leaves. Branched panicles carry many tiny white flowers; fruits are small oval to rounded silicles. Outside its native range it can form dense invasive stands.
Native to Eurasia; introduced and locally invasive in several regions, including North America.
Stout upright stems ending in broad white panicles.
Broad toothed basal leaf; upper leaves are smaller.
Tiny white flower with four petals and six stamens.
Small rounded to oval silicle without a conspicuous apical wing.
Virginia pepperweed
Lepidium virginicum
Virginia peppergrass.

A slender branched annual. Basal leaves, often withered by flowering, are lobed or toothed while stem leaves are narrow. The racemes elongate as they fruit and bear tiny nearly circular silicles with a wing and an apical notch.
Native to North and Central America; introduced in many temperate regions.
Small upright branching annual with narrow racemes of minute flowers and fruits.
Obovate to spatulate basal leaf, often lobed; stem leaves narrow.
Very small white four-petaled flower, usually with two visible stamens.
Flattened round silicle with an apical wing and small notch.
Chinese wolfberry
Lycium chinense
Chinese boxthorn.

A much-branched, sometimes thorny shrub with simple leaves, solitary or clustered. Its flowers are small, mauve and bell-shaped; ripe berries are red and ovoid. It is close to Lycium barbarum, and their features overlap, so identification should combine several characters.
Native to East Asia, especially China; introduced and cultivated elsewhere.
Open shrub with arching thorny branches and sparse foliage.
Small ovate to lanceolate leaf, solitary or in small clusters.
Mauve bell-shaped flower with five short lobes.
Red ovoid berry containing numerous seeds.
Silken pincushion cactus
Mammillaria bombycina
Silken pincushion.

A small clumping Mexican cactus forming globose heads covered in conical tubercles. Each areole bears fine white radial spines mixed with stronger central spines, sometimes hooked; pink flowers form a ring near the apex.
Restricted to central-western Mexico, in dry scrub and rocky places.
Low cactus in tight clusters of globose heads.
Conical tubercle with a woolly areole and spines, including hooked central spines.
Funnel-shaped pink flower near the apex.
Small green elongated berry, becoming more colored at maturity.
Marvel of Peru
Mirabilis jalapa
Four-o’clock flower.

A tuberous perennial native to Mexico, often grown as an annual in cold climates. Branched stems carry opposite broad heart-shaped leaves; trumpet-shaped flowers open in late afternoon. The dry black hard fruits are enclosed by the persistent perianth; seeds should not be eaten.
Native from Mexico to Nicaragua; widely cultivated and naturalized in warm regions.
Bushy branched plant arising from a tuberous root.
Opposite ovate to triangular leaf with a cordate base.
Long-tubed trumpet flower; magenta is shown here, while the species has other colors.
Dry black ovoid fruit with ribs and tubercles.
Mauritian nesocodon
Nesocodon mauritianus
Mauritius bellflower.

A rare shrub from Mauritius, with glaucous foliage and pendent blue-green bells. Red nectar droplets can appear on the corolla; this striking feature is associated with pollination by an endemic gecko. The dry capsule releases small seeds.
Endemic to Mauritius, in humid rocky habitats and cliffs.
Branched subshrub with thick blue-green leaves and pendent flowers.
Thick, glabrous, glaucous elliptic leaf.
Blue-green tubular bell sometimes bearing red nectar droplets outside.
Dry capsule containing many small seeds.
Syrian thistle
Notobasis syriaca
Syrian horse-thistle.

An upright annual thistle with deeply divided spiny leaves marked by silvery-white bands along the veins. Purple flower heads are surrounded by long branched spiny bracts; this feature helps distinguish it from several other Mediterranean thistles.
Eastern Mediterranean and western Asia; common in disturbed ground, pastures and roadsides.
Tall spiny annual with branched stems and several purple heads.
Deeply lobed spiny leaf with silvery marbling.
Purple tubular florets in a head surrounded by branched spiny bracts.
Ribbed achene topped with a feathery pappus.
Common evening-primrose
Oenothera biennis
Evening-primrose.

A tall North American biennial: the first year forms a rosette, followed by an upright flowering stem. Yellow four-petaled flowers open mainly in the evening; the stigma ends in four cross-shaped lobes. The fruit is a long capsule that opens into four valves.
Native to eastern and central North America; naturalized across many temperate regions.
Tall stem with alternate leaves and a long terminal flowering spike.
Narrow lanceolate stem leaf, sessile or shortly petiolate.
Yellow four-petaled flower with eight stamens and four-parted stigma.
Long narrow capsule opening by four valves.
Anomalous bristle-moss
Orthotrichum anomalum
Anomalous orthotrichum.

An acrocarpous moss forming small cushions on limestone rocks and walls. Its leaves press against the stems when dry. At maturity, its brown ribbed capsules raised above the cushion make the species easier to notice.
Cosmopolitan on mineral substrates, especially limestone, walls and gravestones in bright places.
Dense olive-green cushion fixed to stone, with many short setae bearing capsules.
Narrow pointed lanceolate leaf, appressed to the stem when dry.
No flowers: it reproduces by spores; the capsule is capped by a hairy calyptra.
Elongate strongly ribbed capsule; its opening releases spores.
